name: Juice Shop Recon Lab
description: Investigate an intentionally vulnerable OWASP Juice Shop instance from an isolated attacker container, moving from connectivity checks to service discovery, HTTP inspection, and browser confirmation.
learning_objectives: Establish a trustworthy recon baseline by confirming that the attacker can resolve and reach the target host.
Use service discovery to identify the exposed application port and gather evidence that the target is serving web traffic.
Inspect an HTTP response directly so you can connect scan results to real application-layer evidence.
Confirm the relationship between terminal-side recon and the visible browser experience of the OWASP Juice Shop application.
pre_lab_context: OWASP Juice Shop is an intentionally vulnerable training application that behaves like a modern web app. In a real assessment, you would not jump straight into browser interaction without first proving the host is reachable and mapping the exposed service. This lab teaches that disciplined sequence: verify the path, identify the service, inspect the response, then confirm the application visually.
environment_overview: You work from an attacker shell with ping, nmap, and curl available. The target hosts Juice Shop on TCP 3000 inside the isolated lab network, and Secure Stack also provides a forwarded browser URL so you can compare what terminal recon reveals with what the application looks like in a browser.
reflection_prompt: Before you opened Juice Shop in the browser, which terminal-side observation gave you the strongest confidence that the target was a real web application, and why did that matter for the rest of the lab?
lab_takeaways: Connectivity validation gives later recon a trustworthy baseline by proving the attacker can actually reach the target before interpreting failures.
Service discovery transforms a reachable host into a mapped attack surface by showing which port and application behavior deserve deeper attention.
HTTP inspection provides application-layer evidence that is stronger than a port number alone because it shows what the service is actually returning.
Browser confirmation completes the recon story by connecting command-line observations to the visible behavior of the vulnerable application.
prerequisites: Understanding of ICMP, TCP ports, and HTTP
Awareness that the lab is for authorized educational use only
success_criteria: The learner confirms target reachability from the attacker container.
The learner identifies that port 3000 is open and worth deeper inspection.
The learner captures HTTP evidence that the exposed service is the Juice Shop web application.
The learner confirms that the same application is reachable through the forwarded browser URL.

topology.summary: A single attacker container investigates one exposed Juice Shop target across an isolated lab network before validating the application in a browser.

nodes.label: Attacker shell
nodes.details: Use this container to run recon commands, observe responses, and collect evidence.

nodes.label: Juice Shop target
nodes.details: The target hosts the OWASP Juice Shop application on TCP 3000.

connections.label: ICMP, TCP 3000, HTTP, and browser recon path

tasks.title: Verify connectivity
tasks.objective: Confirm that the attacker container can resolve and reach the target host before deeper recon begins.
tasks.instruction: Use a short ICMP probe to verify that the attacker can reach the target host.
tasks.explanation: This opening step proves the lab path is working before you invest effort in scanning or browsing. If the attacker cannot resolve or reach the target cleanly, later recon results become hard to interpret and you risk confusing network problems with application behavior.
what_to_observe: The `target` hostname resolves successfully from the attacker shell.
ICMP replies come back from the target.
The summary shows zero packet loss.
tasks.why_observation_matters: These signals prove the attacker has a working path to the target, which means later scan and HTTP results can be interpreted as service behavior instead of basic connectivity failure.
tasks.learning_takeaway: This confirmed the target was reachable from the attacker shell, which gave you a trustworthy baseline before spending time on deeper service discovery.
tasks.expected_outcome: You should see successful ICMP replies and zero packet loss, confirming that the target alias resolves and the attacker can send traffic across the isolated lab network.
hints: Use the `target` hostname from the attacker shell instead of an IP address.
A short probe count is enough. You only need evidence that the path is working before scanning.
tasks.hint_text: Use the `target` hostname from the attacker shell.
tasks.remediation_text: If ping fails, verify that the lab launched successfully and the target alias is resolvable on the isolated network.
success_criteria: The target responds to ICMP requests from the attacker container.

tasks.title: Identify the exposed web service
tasks.objective: Enumerate the target so you can identify the exposed port and recognize that a web application is likely behind it.
tasks.instruction: Run a version-detection scan against the target to discover the exposed service.
tasks.explanation: Service discovery turns basic reachability into useful recon. This step is not only about seeing that a port is open. It is about learning which service is exposed, which port deserves attention, and whether the next step should move toward application-layer inspection.
what_to_observe: Service or fingerprint details that suggest an HTTP or web application response.
Enough output to justify moving from network recon into HTTP validation.
tasks.why_observation_matters: These observations map the attack surface and tell you where to focus. They convert a live host into a specific application target instead of leaving you with only a generic connectivity result.
tasks.learning_takeaway: This step translated raw reachability into concrete attack-surface evidence by showing which port was exposed and that it behaved like a web service worth deeper inspection.
tasks.expected_outcome: The scan should identify TCP 3000 as open and return service details consistent with a web application that should be validated directly.
hints: Use version detection so the output is useful when you write up evidence later.
If the service is still starting, wait briefly and rerun the scan rather than assuming the host is down.
tasks.hint_text: Use version detection so the scan output is useful for reporting and interpretation.
tasks.remediation_text: If the scan does not show port 3000, confirm the target container is running and wait for the service to finish booting before rescanning.
success_criteria: Port 3000 is identified as open on the target.

tasks.title: Inspect the HTTP response
tasks.objective: Collect direct HTTP evidence that the exposed service is Juice Shop instead of relying on the scan alone.
tasks.instruction: Request the Juice Shop HTTP response directly from the target so you can inspect how the service identifies itself.
tasks.explanation: Once the scan suggests a web service on port 3000, the next step is to validate that assumption with an actual HTTP response. This moves you from port-level evidence into application-layer evidence and helps you connect the exposed service to a real web application identity.
what_to_observe: HTML or response text that references `OWASP Juice Shop`.
Any page structure or headers that show you are talking to a real web application instead of a generic listener.
tasks.why_observation_matters: An HTTP response gives stronger evidence than a port scan alone because it shows what the service actually returns to a client. That is what lets you say the exposed port is serving Juice Shop specifically.
tasks.learning_takeaway: This application-layer check proved that the open port was serving Juice Shop specifically, which is much stronger evidence than a port number alone.
tasks.expected_outcome: The response should succeed and include content that identifies the OWASP Juice Shop application, giving you evidence that the exposed port is serving a real web app.
hints: Capture enough of the response to prove what application is listening on port 3000.
If the response is empty, revisit the scan results and confirm the target service finished booting.
tasks.hint_text: Capture enough of the response to prove what application is listening on port 3000.
tasks.remediation_text: If curl does not return the app, confirm the service is up and revisit the nmap output before trying again.
success_criteria: The learner captures HTTP evidence that identifies the Juice Shop application.

tasks.title: Open the application in a browser
tasks.objective: Confirm that the same service you mapped in the terminal is reachable as a real browser-facing application.
tasks.instruction: Open the published browser URL and confirm that the Juice Shop interface loads.
tasks.explanation: This final step connects terminal recon to the visible application experience. It matters because browser interaction can reveal interface behavior, branding, and user-facing clues that are harder to appreciate from CLI output alone, even when the terminal already proved the service identity.
what_to_observe: The Juice Shop interface loads successfully in the browser.
The visible application matches what the earlier curl response suggested.
The forwarded browser URL reaches the same service you mapped from the attacker shell.
tasks.why_observation_matters: This closes the loop between command-line recon and real user-facing behavior, which is how a reconnaissance narrative becomes complete instead of fragmented.
tasks.learning_takeaway: This browser confirmation showed that the exposed service was not only reachable from the attacker shell but also accessible as a real web application through the forwarded lab URL.
tasks.expected_outcome: The Juice Shop interface should load in a browser, confirming that the same application you identified in the terminal is reachable through the forwarded URL.
expected_evidence: Juice Shop UI loads in the browser
hints: Use the browser URL returned by the launcher rather than guessing the host port.
If the page fails to load, confirm the target container is still running and the forwarded port remains published.
tasks.hint_text: Use the browser URL returned by the lab launcher.
tasks.remediation_text: If the browser does not load, confirm the launcher returned a valid host port and that the target container is still running.
success_criteria: The learner manually confirms that the Juice Shop UI is reachable.
